video_title: Write, Change, Recall, Forget: MongoDB's Pete Johnson on How Retrieval Drives Agent Performance
gist: Pete Johnson, field CTO of AI at MongoDB, argues that cost-adjusted agent performance now hinges on retrieval quality, after enterprises whipsawed from forced RAG to 'RAG is dead' to token maxing and back, with Uber burning its 2026 token budget in 13 weeks as the cautionary catalyst. He details MongoDB's retrieval stack (hybrid search with rank/score fusion, $rerank, Voyage AI embeddings with contextualized chunking, Matryoshka dimensions and shared embedding spaces), insists embeddings are not commoditized, and frames agent memory as a write-change-recall-forget loop where forgetting is the unsolved problem. He also reports that the two most sophisticated AI customers he met in 2026 were in Mexico City and Sao Paulo, not the US.

insights.claim: Database design paradigms are downstream of which hardware resource is scarce: SQL normalization was invented in 1970 when storage was the most expensive of memory/compute/storage, while MongoDB's 2007 denormalized document model assumed storage was cheap and time was scarce.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Use the same lens on AI infra: today's scarce resource is context-window tokens and retrieval quality, which predicts where the next architectural winners sit.

insights.claim: Denormalizing a record so it can be fetched in a single disk read instead of three joined table reads is the core mechanical source of MongoDB's speed advantage, not marketing.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Latency advantages persist wherever per-call round trips multiply, e.g. agent loops issuing many retrievals per task.

insights.claim: MongoDB ended fiscal 2026 at roughly $2.5B revenue, which is only about 2-3% of a $100-110B total database market, and it is deployed in roughly 75% of the Fortune 500.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Low share of a huge TAM plus deep enterprise footprint frames the bull case: land-and-expand into AI workloads rather than net-new logo acquisition.
insights.quote: we're in like 75% of the Fortune 500

insights.claim: MongoDB is schema-flexible rather than schemaless, a distinction that matters because documents in the same collection can carry different shapes, which is precisely what made bolting a vector array onto existing documents trivial.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Explains why incumbents with flexible document models can add vector capability faster than standalone vector DBs can add durability, sharding and security.
insights.quote: It's not that we're schemalists. It's that we're schema flexible

insights.claim: Enterprises are split between per-workload database selection and all-in single-vendor strategies, with the deciding variable usually being greenfield-vs-brownfield mix and where existing engineering talent already sits, not technical merit.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Vendor displacement in databases is talent- and portfolio-gated, so incumbency is stickier than feature comparisons suggest.

insights.claim: Enterprise retrieval strategy has round-tripped three times in about two years: forced RAG under GPT-4-class context limits, then 'RAG is dead' when million-token contexts arrived, then a token-maxing phase, and now RAG is again a top enterprise priority because naive context stuffing costs multiple dollars per call.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Narrative volatility this fast means retrieval-infrastructure sentiment is a mean-reverting trade; buy the 'RAG is dead' drawdowns.

insights.claim: Uber burned through its entire 2026 token budget in 13 weeks, a widely covered incident that materially shifted enterprise attitudes away from token maxing toward selective retrieval.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: A named, dated blowup is the catalyst that turns retrieval optimization from nice-to-have into a budget line; expect FinOps-for-tokens to become a category.
insights.quote: in the wake of what happened to Uber earlier in the year with them burning through their token budget for 2026 and 13 weeks

insights.claim: The token-maxing idea went from first being discussed in early March to being over as a conversation piece by April, illustrating that AI architecture fads now complete a full hype-and-death cycle in roughly one month.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Underwriting periods for AI infra theses must be compressed; a product roadmap built on a one-quarter-old consensus is already stale.
insights.quote: Token maxing first got mentioned in like early March and by April it was over as like a conversation piece

insights.claim: Academic work indicates roughly the first 7K and last 7K tokens of a context window carry most of the influence, so stuffing the middle with a million tokens actively degrades answer quality rather than merely costing money.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Retrieval quality has a functional payoff on top of the cost payoff, which strengthens pricing power for retrieval tooling versus pure cost-cutting tools.
insights.quote: the first 7K and like the last 7K tokens are the most important and the stuff that's in between can end up just muddying and confusing the LLM

insights.claim: The emerging enterprise design goal is not maximizing context but selecting the right ~200K tokens for each agentic loop, which reframes context management as a search problem rather than a capacity problem.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Every incremental context-window expansion by model labs increases, not decreases, demand for retrieval and ranking infrastructure.
insights.quote: what if I could choose just the right 200,000 for this agentic loop?

insights.claim: Retrieval quality has become a third purchase driver for databases alongside speed and scale, specifically because of agentic architectures that emerged in the second half of 2026 and did not exist in the first half.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: A new buying criterion means a new competitive axis; vendors without embedding/reranking assets are structurally disadvantaged in AI-era database bake-offs.

themes.theme: The Retrieval Stack: Embeddings, Rerankers, Chunking

insights.claim: Embedding models are not commoditized despite widespread belief to the contrary, with top models delivering up to a 14% retrieval-quality improvement over popular cloud-default embedders on the RTEB benchmark.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: If true, embedding quality is a defensible product line rather than a race to zero, supporting acquisitions and pricing in the embedding layer.
insights.quote: Most people think embedding models are commoditized, and that is not true.

insights.claim: Anthropic ships no embedding model of its own and recommends Voyage AI, which MongoDB owns, giving MongoDB a distribution channel inside the Claude developer ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: A frontier-lab endorsement is a durable go-to-market moat for the embedding layer; watch whether Anthropic ever builds its own embedder.
insights.quote: Anthropic does not have an embedding model in market. They recommend us. It's a great recommendation.

insights.claim: Adding a reranker on top of any embedding model typically yields a 5-10% retrieval-quality boost without touching the underlying data, making it the cheapest available quality lever.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Rerankers are a high-ROI, low-switching-cost insert point; incumbents that bundle them capture that margin.
insights.quote: you can get like a 5 to 10% boost at your retrieval quality just by using a re-ranker

insights.claim: The default starting stack for most AI builders is Postgres with pgvector plus whichever embedding model matches their cloud (Gemini on Google, OpenAI on Azure), and that default only breaks down at roughly 100,000 vectors.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: 100K vectors is the concrete trigger point for upsell into specialized retrieval infrastructure; a useful funnel metric for the whole category.
insights.quote: that typically comes at about 100,000 vectors is when is what I mean by scale

insights.claim: Contextualized chunking breaks the traditional trade-off curve where retrieval quality rises with chunk size then degrades, by sending the target sentence and its surrounding context as two strings that collapse into a single vector.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Removing the chunk-size tuning loop lowers the skill floor for agent builders, expanding the addressable developer base for retrieval products.
insights.quote: you can flip that script

insights.claim: Voyage shipped contextualized chunking v3 last summer and v4 within the last six weeks, a cadence that shows the embedding layer is still improving fast rather than settling.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Rapid version cadence supports the non-commoditization thesis and argues against locking long-term contracts on any single embedder.
insights.quote: we released version three of that last summer. We just released four of that in the last six weeks

insights.claim: Voyage models use Matryoshka-style ordered dimensions so a team can truncate a 1024-dimension vector to 512 and test immediately, instead of re-embedding the entire corpus at the new dimensionality.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: This directly reduces the compute cost of dimension tuning, a real switching-cost advantage over embedders that force full re-embedding.

insights.claim: MongoDB's January release of four version-4 text embedding models shares one embedding space across all four sizes, including a free open-weight 'nano' model, so teams can embed the corpus with the large model and run development queries locally at zero token cost.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Free local dev inference is a land-grab tactic that seeds paid production usage; a template other infra vendors may copy.
insights.quote: in January we released four versions of the of the version four of the text model

insights.claim: MongoDB's product cadence has moved retrieval work into single API round trips: rank fusion and score fusion combine lexical and vector search in one aggregation-pipeline call, and $rerank shipped in the spring folds reranking into the same call.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Round-trip consolidation is how a database vendor absorbs margin from standalone reranking and orchestration startups.

insights.claim: MongoDB's auto embeddings feature automatically re-embeds and re-indexes any document whose designated attribute changes, eliminating customer-maintained embedding pipelines entirely.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Each such feature deletes a category of third-party glue tooling; check ETL/embedding-pipeline startups for disruption risk.

insights.claim: MongoDB's roadmap is driven by observing what customers already build by hand and then absorbing it, as with 2020's Atlas Search after seeing customers self-host Apache Lucene clusters alongside their MongoDB deployments.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: This is an explicit playbook for serial absorption of adjacent point solutions; anticipate the next absorption target from what customers currently bolt on.
insights.quote: there's two kinds of developers. There's those that love MongoDB and there's ones that haven't tried us.

themes.theme: Agent Memory Architecture & the Forgetting Problem

insights.claim: The general pattern for agent memory is a four-verb loop of write, change, recall and forget, and forgetting is currently the unsolved hard part because memories carry a half-life that naive systems do not model.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Whoever productizes forgetting/decay owns a defensible layer; today it is a homegrown gap in every enterprise stack.
insights.quote: Write, change, recall, forget.

insights.claim: Naive agent memory implementations dump every response from the session into short-term memory and every session from the last three days into long-term memory, which produces both token cost blowups and degraded relevance.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: The failure mode is universal enough to create a real product category between the model and the database.

insights.claim: A new memory type called taxonomic memory is appearing in Fortune 500 deployments, storing vertical- or company-specific terminology and retrieving only the five relevant terms per agent loop rather than injecting all hundred.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Domain-specific vocabulary is a proprietary data asset; taxonomic memory is how it gets monetized inside agents.
insights.quote: there's a new memory type called taxonomic memory

insights.claim: Sophisticated memory systems now expose a token budget as the query interface, so the application asks for 'the best 50K tokens' and the memory layer decides the mix across memory types.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Token-budget-as-API is the interface convention to watch; it standardizes how retrieval vendors get measured.

insights.claim: Application developers now carry a second responsibility they did not have with simple RAG: writing the agent's answer back into the memory system for curation, and advanced systems share those curated memories across users in the same job type.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Shared memory across same-role users creates a compounding data network effect inside enterprises, raising switching costs.

insights.claim: Using additional LLM passes to compress or categorize memory before the main call is an architectural anti-pattern, because it re-adds the token cost and latency that the memory system was supposed to remove; embedders and rerankers are the low-cost tools for that job.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Bearish read on 'LLM-as-memory-manager' startups; bullish on cheap embedder/reranker primitives.
insights.quote: I would worry about any memory architecture that instead of relying on lower cost embedders and rerankers is relying on multiple passes of the LLM

insights.claim: Practical enterprise memory increasingly uses a hybrid graph-then-vector shape: a graph structure two to twelve levels deep for categorization, then a vector search within the leaf node, commonly seen in retail product catalogs.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Demand is for graph-lite inside a general database, not dedicated graph databases, which caps the standalone graph-DB opportunity.

insights.claim: ElevenLabs is described as MongoDB's biggest customer and runs a micro-agent architecture with multiple small agents per customer, making it a live reference case for memory at agent scale.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Voice/audio AI companies are becoming top-decile database consumers, a demand signal for infrastructure exposure to that vertical.
insights.quote: There's a company called 11 Labs out there.

insights.claim: Memory systems commonly retain stale intentions, keeping abandoned projects as open threads for months, which shows that recall without decay actively corrupts an agent's model of the user.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that memory quality, not memory capacity, is the binding constraint on agent usefulness.

themes.theme: Enterprise AI Adoption, ROI & Problem Selection

insights.claim: Failed enterprise AI ROI is usually a problem-selection failure rather than a technology failure, and the correct filter is the intersection of the company's top 10-15 business problems, where good data exists, and where metrics already exist.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: A diagnostic for screening AI vendors and corporate AI programs: no pre-existing metric means no provable ROI and likely no renewal.
insights.quote: if you don't already have metrics for how something is performing, you won't know if it got better

insights.claim: Bad data quality and bad security posture are not solved by AI adoption; they are amplified by it, meaning AI deployment raises rather than lowers the return on prior data governance investment.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Supports demand for data-quality and security tooling as a complement to, not a substitute for, AI spend.
insights.quote: Things like bad data quality and bad security posture don't get solved by AI, they get amplified by AI.

insights.claim: Enterprises cluster into three AI maturity camps: bought a single tool and declared the strategy done, stuck in PoC purgatory with weak ROI, and advanced buyers optimizing memory systems via platform purchases or homegrown builds.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Sales cycles and TAM per camp differ sharply; the third camp is where infrastructure spend actually lands.

insights.claim: Call centers are the archetypal enterprise AI beachhead specifically because cost-per-call and call volume are already instrumented for bonus purposes, allowing immediate back-of-envelope ROI attribution.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Predicts where AI budget concentrates first: any function with pre-existing KPI instrumentation, not necessarily the highest-value function.

insights.claim: Lines of code is a terrible productivity metric for AI-assisted development, and the metric that actually matters is time from idea to production deployment.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Reframes how to evaluate coding-assistant vendor claims and enterprise developer-productivity disclosures.
insights.quote: lines of code is a terrible metric to judge the productivity of a set of developers off of

insights.claim: Most Fortune 500 companies are still deploying employee-facing AI with a human in the loop rather than autonomous customer-facing AI, because a leaked employee salary is survivable while a customer seeing another customer's data is a fireable executive-level incident.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Sets the realistic pace of customer-facing AI disruption in large enterprises and explains why SMBs move faster.
insights.quote: the riskreward is higher for customerf facing use cases than it is for employee facing use cases

insights.claim: Voice AI agents have already reached single-location small businesses, with a one-location Detroit pizza shop answering its phone with a capable AI agent that handled the happy path well but broke under adversarial questioning.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: SMB voice AI diffusion is running ahead of Fortune 500 customer-facing deployment, inverting the usual enterprise-first adoption assumption.

insights.claim: There is still no LAMP stack or React equivalent for agents because the industry is only 18-24 months into building them, which means no enterprise can buy an agent platform and deploy it without meaningful custom work.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Services and integration margin stays high for now; a standardized agent stack emerging is the signal that margins compress.
insights.quote: There's there's no lampstack for agents yet in the way that we have with web development.

insights.claim: Databases have 60 years of accumulated practice while agents have roughly 18 months, so current agent best practices should be treated as provisional rather than as durable architecture.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Argues against long-duration bets on any specific agent architecture and for bets on the primitives underneath them.
insights.quote: we've been building databases for 60 years. We've been building agents for like 18 months, man.

insights.claim: More developers will build AI agents in the next three years than did in the last three, which is why vendors are competing on lowering the learning curve rather than on raw capability.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Developer-experience simplification, not benchmark wins, is the stated competitive battleground for infrastructure vendors.
insights.quote: more developers will build AI agents in the next three years than did in the last 3 years

themes.theme: Defensibility: Incumbent Platforms vs Point Solutions

insights.claim: MongoDB acquired Voyage AI for about $220 million, less than 1% of its roughly $30 billion market cap, buying the model layer rather than any of the many available vector-database startups.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: The relative price signals where value accrued: infrastructure incumbents captured the storage layer cheaply and paid only for scarce model talent.
insights.quote: the price at even at $220 million

insights.claim: Adding vector search to an existing document database was straightforward because a vector is just an array of floats stored as another attribute, which is why incumbents inherited sharding, replication, encryption and multi-cloud deployment for free while standalone vector DBs must rebuild all of it.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Core bear case for standalone vector-database startups; the enterprise-grade features are the moat, not the index.

insights.claim: The counter-argument for vector-database startups is that most data entering vector databases has never been in any database before, sitting instead in data lakes, SharePoint and unstructured document piles, so the category expands the market rather than dividing the existing one.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: If true, vector DB TAM is additive and not a zero-sum fight with incumbents; test it against incumbents' AI-workload growth rates.
insights.quote: most of the data that is coming into our vector database has never been in a database before at all

insights.claim: MongoDB confirms a genuine phase shift in what data gets indexed, with video, audio and unstructured PDFs entering databases for the first time because vector similarity search works where lexical search never could.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Multimodal embedding support expands storage and compute demand into previously dark data, a structural volume tailwind for infrastructure.

insights.claim: MongoDB's consolidation pitch is a single console for core data, vector data, embedding models and rerankers including unified API key management, positioning bundling as the main defense against best-of-breed point solutions.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Classic suite-versus-point-solution dynamic; watch whether enterprises pay a quality premium for standalone embedders or accept bundled good-enough.

insights.claim: MongoDB offers three deployment forms, community (self-support, self-operate), enterprise advanced (mostly on-prem, vendor support), and Atlas (managed on AWS, Google or Azure), with the vector and search features gated to the managed Atlas tier.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: AI features gating to the managed tier is the mechanism converting on-prem installed base into higher-margin cloud revenue.

insights.claim: MCP went from publication on the Monday before Thanksgiving to universal competitor adoption as a protocol by the following March, one of the fastest standards adoptions in software history.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Protocol standardization at that speed compresses the window for proprietary integration moats in the agent tooling layer.
insights.quote: MC published MCP on like Monday before Thanksgiving two years ago and by March all of their competitors had embraced it as a protocol

insights.claim: Infrastructure vendors now compete to be the database that agents recommend by default, shipping self-hosted MCP servers inside Atlas and six to eight agent skills as curated markdown system prompts for tasks like data modeling and operations optimization.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Agent recommendation is becoming a distribution channel comparable to SEO or app-store ranking; early movers may lock in default status.

insights.claim: Documentation is being rewritten as machine-consumable artifacts, with previously human-facing playbooks repackaged as markdown skill files fed to agents, which changes how developer mindshare is won.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Developer-relations spend is shifting from human content to agent-consumable content; a leading indicator of who wins the next cohort of builders.

insights.claim: After visiting seven countries and roughly 100 customers in one year, the two most sophisticated AI customers encountered were in Mexico City and Sao Paulo, not the United States, contradicting the widespread assumption of US leadership.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: If frontier enterprise AI adoption is genuinely global, investable AI-transformation exposure is not confined to US-listed adopters.
insights.quote: the two most sophisticated customers I talked to this year were in Mexico City and Sa Paulo

insights.claim: Geographic barriers to AI capability have collapsed because nearly every country now has at least one hyperscaler data center, unlike the cloud and mobile waves where missing local infrastructure meant being locked out.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Removes the geographic lag that historically made emerging-market tech adoption a delayed derivative of US adoption.
insights.quote: there's a presumption in other countries that the US is ahead and doing things that other people are not and I found the opposite to be true

insights.claim: The international lead is attributed to the absence of barriers outside the US rather than any conservatism inside US companies, meaning it reflects democratized access rather than a leapfrog over legacy investment.
insights.speaker: Pete Johnson
insights.so_what: Frames non-US AI adoption as a durable structural shift rather than a temporary catch-up cycle.
